title: Minute SLI Hardening and Dashboard Surgery Playbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for converting noisy minute-level signals into hardened SLIs and surgically simplifying dashboards used by oncall and SRE. Objective: reduce alert thrash, lower MTTI for real regressions, and remove panels that cost queries without operator value. This is an ops-first doc — decision steps and small experiments, not a long design treatise.

Scope:
- Focus: text-generation token-serving paths (hosted + dedicated) and their minute-level SLI surfaces (TFTT, tail token latency, kv-cache hit warmth).
- Exclude: long-term business metrics (billing/usage aggregation), embedding pipelines (separate team).
- Audience: oncall, observability owners, product infra, and engineering owners for serving runtime.

Summary of changes we propose (top-level):
1) Define 3 minute-level SLIs with explicit rollup rules and noise filters.
2) Introduce trace-anchor fields (session_id, model_variant, cache_warmth_bin) to every span for deterministic correlation.
3) Prune 20% of dashboard panels that are derivable or very high-cost; retain 8 compact operator micro-panels.
4) Add a short rollback mechanism for alert aggressiveness (feature-flagged guardrail).

Definitions (quick):
- TFTT: Time to first token (ms) measured from request receive -> first token emission.
- Token tail p95/p99: per-token emission time quantiles across the minute window.
- KV-warmth index: minute-aggregated fraction of requests that hit prefix/KV cache (0..1).
- Minute SLI: a ratio computed per-minute, then rolled up as a burn-rate aware SLO. Example: minute_bad = count(minutes where p99>200ms) / total_minutes.

Minute-level SLI specs (concrete):
1) TFTT-successful-minute-sli
- Definition: For each minute, an inference request is "good" if TFTT < 120ms and generation started within 2s, otherwise "bad".
- Measurement: sample up to 1k requests per minute per cluster (biased toward user-facing routes).
- Rollup: minute_good_ratio = good_count / sampled_count. Use inverse weighting for low-volume routes (see runbook).
- Alert rule (initial): alert if minute_good_ratio < 0.98 for 3 consecutive minutes AND global traffic > baseline threshold.

2) Token-tail-minute-sli
- Definition: For each minute compute p99 token emission latency across all tokens (exclude system tokens).
- Measurement: approximate via histogram buckets emitted by runtime (avoid shipping raw traces).
- Threshold: p99_token_latency > 200ms flagged as bad-minute.
- Alert rule: fire when bad-minute occurs in 5/6 minutes in a 10-minute sliding window for high-traffic clusters.

3) KV-cache-warmth-minute-sli
- Definition: minute fraction of requests that used a warm KV prefix cache.
- Measurement: runtime emits per-request boolean flag cache_hit. Aggregate by minute.
- Threshold: warmth < 0.6 triggers investigation but is not a page by itself — tied to TFTT degradation.

Trace anchoring and span contract (developer-facing):
- Every root span MUST set these tags: session_id, request_id, model_name, model_variant, route, customer_tier, kv_warmth_bin (hot/warm/cold).
- Child spans should propagate request_id and model_variant.
- For token emission spans include token_index and token_latency_ms. Avoid storing full tokens.
- Annotate fallback flows: fallback_model and fallback_reason.

Tracing sampling policy (minute-focused):
- Baseline: 0.5% sampling for all requests.
- Spike policy: when minute token-tail p99 crosses 2x baseline, ramp to 5% for 10 minutes limited to 500 traces/min to bound cost.
- Error bias: always sample 100% of spans for requests that returned 5xx or hit fallback.

Dashboard surgery steps (practical, two-week sprint):
Week 1 (triage + temp flags):
- Inventory (day 1): run current dashboard cost query to list panels by monthly query cost and last-90-day usage.
- Owner mapping (day 1-2): assign an owner to every panel; unclaimed panels default to "candidate-prune".
- Quick wins (day 3): remove duplicate panels and ones with stale queries (>90 days unchanged).
- Add the 3 new minute SLI panels (compact sparkline + last-minute card + burn-rate mini-table).

Week 2 (hardening + rollout):
- Replace noisy minute panels with sampled versions or use derived aggregates (e.g., histogram -> p99).
- Implement trace anchor annotations and add a link from minute-SLI panel to trace search with prefilled tags.
- Add alert automation: a feature flag gate that controls whether an SLI can page.
- Run a 48-hour experiment with lowered alert sensitivity and document incident capture rate.

Panel cost-reduction guidelines (practical):
- Prefer pre-aggregated minute buckets emitted by backend instead of heavy ad-hoc queries over raw events.
- If a panel pulls >100k rows/minute, switch to derived metric or reduce refresh to 1m with caching.
- Coalesce multiple related panels into a single compact multi-series panel.

Operator micro-dashboard (keeper panels):
- Global minute-SLI summary (TFTT, token-p99, kv-warmth) 1-row sparklines.
- Hot cluster map (top 5 clusters by error rate).
- Recent heavy traces (linked list: 50 most recent sampled traces matching minute-bad anchors).
- Rollout watch: model-variant success ratio for last 60 minutes.
- Cost-backstop: panel showing top 3 queries by billed rows for the dashboard.

Rollout checklist (pre-deploy):
- Runtime emits the new tags and histogram buckets (feature branch tested).
- Dashboards referenced in PR and have owners assigned.
- Alert feature flag exists and defaulted off for production; small cadence pilot enabled.
- Oncall runbook updated and linked in the pager text with quick mitigation steps.

Runbook excerpt (for minute-SLI TFTT page):
1) Acknowledge alert.
2) Check global minute-SLI panel for co-occurring token p99 or KV-warmth dips.
3) Open linked trace search (auto-prefilled model_variant + minute window).
4) If traces show consistent model variant slow inflight: rollback to previous variant via rollout console OR reduce concurrency on that variant.
5) If kv-warmth is low: trigger KV prefetch job (ops playbook) and monitor TFTT.
6) If no clear signal: escalate to serving-runtime oncall.

Experimentation protocol (metrics to capture during 48h):
- Number of pages (pre vs post) normalized by traffic.
- Time to detection (MTTI) for incidents that impact user-visible latency.
- False positive rate measured via post-incident triage labels.
- Dashboard query cost delta.

Examples (operationally useful queries) — pseudo-SQL for metrics backend:
- minute_tftt_good_ratio: SELECT minute, sum(case when tftt_ms<120 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/count(*) as good_ratio FROM inference_requests WHERE cluster='us-east' GROUP BY minute
- minute_token_p99: SELECT minute, histogram_quantile(0.99, token_latency_hist) FROM token_latency_buckets WHERE model='redwood-13b' GROUP BY minute
- kv_warmth: SELECT minute, sum(case when cache_hit THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/count(*) as warmth FROM inference_requests GROUP BY minute

Open questions (to decide in sprint retro):
- Sampling caps: what is an acceptable ceiling for trace ramp-ups per cluster?
- Low-volume route weighting: should we exclude routes < 100 requests/min from minute alerts?
- Warmth threshold tuning: is 0.6 the right floor or too conservative?

Owner and next steps:
- Observability lead: Aisha Patel (doc owner)
- Runtime instrumentation owner: Priya Raman (ensure tags + histograms)
- Dashboard owner and PR shepherd: Luca Moretti
- Oncall & SRE feedback loop: Samir Khan

Immediate actions (today):
- Runtime owners: add session_id + model_variant + token_latency_hist to feature branch trace schema (PR link in linked_artifacts).
- Dashboard owners: run panel inventory query and start mapping owners (tag panels in dashboard repo).
- Oncall: prepare a short playbook snippet to attach to alert templates.

Appendix: short taxonomy for kv_warmth_bin (runtime):
- hot: cache_hit rate > 0.85 in the last 5 minutes
- warm: cache_hit rate between 0.5 and 0.85
- cold: cache_hit rate < 0.5

Notes and tone: this is intentionally pragmatic. We expect multiple micro-iterations. The aim is to create deterministic anchors that let operators move quickly from minute-level signal to a small set of causal hypotheses (cache, model-variant, infra). Keep instrumentation lightweight and prioritize trace sampling caps to control cost.
